conflicts.point: Whether federal regulatory agencies should enforce pre-training compute licenses and administrative boundaries or rely exclusively on post-deployment liability and enforcement of existing civil rights and labor statutes.

positions.stance: Federal oversight should avoid pre-training compute limits entirely, using modular verification and post-deployment enforcement to support rapid technological iteration and open-source development.
Federal regulators must establish pre-training governance mechanisms and tiered audit requirements to prevent irreversible risks before autonomous capabilities are locked into model weights.
Federal agencies should abandon speculative compute limits and instead enforce strict data provenance, algorithmic accountability, and labor protections against documented present-day harms.

verdicts.conflict: Whether federal regulatory agencies should enforce pre-training compute licenses and administrative boundaries or rely exclusively on post-deployment liability and enforcement of existing civil rights and labor statutes.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position correctly identifies the irreversibility of frontier model weights, but the accelerationist position correctly notes that static compute baselines quickly become obsolete due to algorithmic efficiency gains. Neither camp provides a complete framework that simultaneously prevents catastrophic misuse and preserves open-source innovation without significant regulatory capture.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Demonstrated empirical evidence that dynamic compute thresholds can successfully track algorithmic efficiency gains without creating insurmountable compliance costs for smaller developers.
